source.citation: "Journal of Lieutenant James Strode Swearingen", printed as Appendix I in Milo Milton Quaife, Chicago and the Old Northwest, 1673-1835: A Study of the Evolution of the Northwestern Frontier, together with a History of Fort Dearborn (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1913), pp. 373-377. The Chicago entry, Wednesday 17 August 1803, runs across pp. 376-377.

transcribes.work: Journal of Lieutenant James Strode Swearingen, kept on the march from Detroit to Chicago in temporary command of the company sent to establish the first Fort Dearborn; entry for Wednesday 17 August 1803, the day of arrival

what_it_does_not_supply: any surface gradient, and therefore no evidence for or against a level water surface as a measurement
any measurement at the forks — every figure here is taken 1.2 miles downstream at the fort site
any measurement after 1803, and the 1833-34 harbour cut removed the condition the witness gives for the river standing dead
a bank height for the modelled quadrant: 'quite low' is qualitative and cannot promote a confidence
the north bank's height as a number — the 6 ft widely quoted from this passage is arithmetic performed on a hedged estimate by later writers, not a figure Swearingen wrote
any planform: the journal draws nothing and no geometry is traced from it
what_it_supplies: channel width and depth at the Fort Dearborn site in August 1803, from a witness standing there
the height of the south (fort) bank at that point, about 8 feet
that the north bank was lower, by an estimate made by eye and stated as a maximum of two feet
that the river above the fort had quite low banks — the only statement here about the reach this project models
that the pre-cut river was dead water, and the witness's reason for it: the mouth was stopped up by sand washing in from the lake
the distance from the fort site down to the natural mouth in 1803: half a mile
